passage: Monday. In the queue at the stationery shop, Dolma's heart suddenly started pounding so hard she could hear it. The shelves tilted. Her hands tingled. Something terrible is happening, she thought, I'm going to collapse. She ran outside and gripped the railing. Ten minutes later it faded, leaving her shaky and confused. Two weeks later. She hadn't gone back to that shop. She took the long way to tuition to avoid the market. She'd started skipping the crowded school canteen. Her world was getting smaller, and she knew it. The Saturday after. She told her friend Sunaina everything, and Sunaina came with her to tell her mother. At the clinic the doctor checked her carefully and explained what had happened in her body. "It's frightening, but it passes. We can work on the fear of the next one."

qa.q: Where did Dolma feel the sudden wave of fear?
qa.a: In the queue at the stationery shop.

qa.q: What did Dolma think was happening during the attack?
qa.a: She felt terrified, thinking something terrible was happening and that she was going to collapse.

qa.q: What turning point came on the Saturday?
qa.a: She told Sunaina, who went with her to tell her mother, and a doctor explained what happens in her body.

qa.q: How might Sunaina have felt hearing Dolma's story?
qa.a: Sunaina may have been worried for Dolma, and glad Dolma trusted her enough to share it.

passage: "Jatin, you said your heart went crazy in the exam hall, like you were dying? Sit. Your Tarun Chacha knows that feeling. I was sixteen, at the cinema with friends. In the middle of the film my heart started hammering. I couldn't breathe properly. Everything went far away, like looking down a tunnel. I was sure something terrible was happening. I ran out into the lobby. After a few minutes it slowly passed, and I sat there shaking. After that, I stopped going to the cinema. Then I stopped going to cricket in case it happened in front of everyone. My life got smaller and smaller, all out of fear of the next one. Your Dadi finally took me to a doctor. He explained it was panic, frightening but not dangerous, and it passes. That changed everything. So tomorrow, we'll tell your parents and see the doctor together."

qa.q: Where was Tarun Chacha when his first attack happened?
qa.a: At the cinema with friends, in the middle of the film.

qa.q: What was Tarun afraid of after the first attack?
qa.a: He was afraid it would happen again in front of everyone, so he feared the next one.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Tarun Chacha's story, and why did it help?
qa.a: Dadi took him to a doctor, who explained it was panic, frightening but not dangerous, and that it passes; understanding that changed everything.

qa.q: How might Dadi have felt watching young Tarun's life get smaller?
qa.a: Dadi was likely worried to see him give up the cinema and cricket, which is why she finally took him to a doctor.

passage: Dhruv, sixteen, was on the crowded local bus to the town school when it hit. His heart hammered, the world tilted and a voice in his head screamed that something terrible was happening. He pushed off at the next stop and sat under a neem tree, sweating, sure he was dying. After some minutes it faded. Since then he has walked the five kilometres every morning, leaving at dawn, too afraid to board the bus again. His aunt Uma, who runs the tea stall at the crossroads, noticed him trudging past each day. "Beta, why aren't you on the bus?" When he told her, she sat him down with a glass of water. "That sounds frightening. Let's tell your father and go to the doctor at the health centre."

qa.q: Where did Dhruv sit after getting off the bus?
qa.a: He sat under a neem tree.

qa.q: How did Dhruv feel during the wave on the bus?
qa.a: He felt terrified and sure he was dying, with a hammering heart and the world tilting.

qa.q: What sensible step does Uma suggest?
qa.a: She suggests telling his father and seeing the doctor at the health centre.

qa.q: How might Uma have felt seeing Dhruv walk past every day?
qa.a: She was probably puzzled and concerned, which is why she asked him why he wasn't on the bus.

passage:
On a crowded tram in Gothenburg, Anders was scrolling through a football video when his heart began to pound. The carriage seemed to tilt. His hands tingled, and a thought rushed in: something terrible is happening.
He grabbed the pole. His friend Lucia said, "Anders? You've gone white."
"I think I'm dying," he whispered.
He got off at the next stop and sat on a bench, gulping air. Slowly, the pounding eased. The world stopped tilting. It passed.
But the next morning he told his mum he'd walk the long way to school. And the next. By Friday he'd stopped going to the shopping centre with friends too, just in case. Lucia noticed. "You can't walk everywhere forever," she said gently. "Tell your mum what really happened."

qa.q: What was Anders watching when his heart began to pound?
qa.a: A football video.

qa.q: What was Anders feeling on the tram?
qa.a: He felt terrified, with a pounding heart, dizziness and a sense that something terrible was happening, even that he was dying.

qa.q: What went wrong after the attack, and what small step does Lucia suggest?
qa.a: His fear of another one made him avoid the tram and the shopping centre; Lucia suggests telling his mum what really happened so he can get help.

qa.q: How does Lucia see Anders's new habit of walking everywhere?
qa.a: She notices and feels concerned that his life is getting smaller, and wants him to get support.

grounding: Anders has a sudden wave of fear with a pounding heart and dizziness that passes, but fear of the next one begins to shrink his life.
